patient_summary:
Hello there! I'll explain what happened in a way that's easy to understand. You had a doctor visit because you were having ear pain on the right side. The doctor wanted to look inside your throat to find out what was causing the pain. They did a special procedure called a microsuspension direct laryngoscopy, which means they used a tiny camera to look at your vocal cords and the back of your throat.

They gave you medicine to help you sleep during the procedure. After you were asleep, they put a tube in your nose to help you breathe. They then used a special tool to look at your throat and vocal cords. They saw that your right vocal cord was a little red, but there were no other problems. They also saw a small, soft bump on the right side of your throat. They took a tiny piece of tissue from this bump to send to the lab to check it out.

They also saw some small bumps on the back of your throat, so they took a tiny piece of that tissue too. Once they were done, they cleaned your throat and took you to the recovery room. You were awake and doing well when you left.

You should feel better soon. If you have any pain or swelling, or if you have any other problems, you should call your doctor. They will let you know what the lab results say. Remember to take any medicine they give you as instructed. If you have any questions, you can always ask your doctor or nurse.
caregiver_checklist: Give the patient a dose of pain medication as prescribed.
Check the patient's vital signs every hour for the first 24 hours.
Watch for signs of infection such as fever, redness, or increased pain.
Call the doctor if the patient develops a fever over 100.4°F.
Schedule a follow-up appointment in 2 weeks for a postoperative check-up.
Check the patient's incision site for signs of infection or bleeding.
Watch for signs of airway obstruction or difficulty breathing.
Call the doctor if the patient experiences difficulty swallowing or drooling.
Schedule a biopsy pathology report review appointment in 1-2 weeks.
Watch for signs of voice changes or hoarseness.
Call the doctor if the patient experiences persistent pain or swelling.

source_text: PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSES:,1.  Fullness in right base of the tongue.,2.  Chronic right ear otalgia.,POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: , Pending pathology.,PROCEDURE PERFORMED: , Microsuspension direct laryngoscopy with biopsy.,ANESTHESIA: , General.,INDICATION:,  This is a 50-year-old female who presents to the office with a chief complaint of ear pain on the right side.  Exact etiology of her ear pain had not been identified.  A fiberoptic examination had been performed in the office.  Upon examination, she was noted to have fullness in the right base of her tongue.  She was counseled on the risks, benefits, and alternatives to surgery and consented to such.,PROCEDURE: , After informed consent was obtained, the patient was brought to the Operative Suite where she was placed in supine position.  General endotracheal tube intubation was delivered by the Department of Anesthesia.  The patient was rotated 90 degrees away where a shoulder roll was placed.  A tooth guard was then placed to protect the upper dentition.  The Dedo laryngoscope was then inserted into the oral cavity.  It was advanced on the right lateral pharyngeal wall until the epiglottis was brought into view.  At this point, it was advanced underneath the epiglottis until the vocal cords were seen.  At this point, it was suspended via the Lewy suspension arm from the Mayo stand.  At this point, the Zeiss microscope with a 400 mm lens was brought into the surgical field.  Inspection of the vocal cords underneath the microscope revealed them to be white and glistening without any mucosal abnormalities.  It should be mentioned that the right vocal cord did appear to be slightly more hyperemic, however, there were no mucosal abnormalities identified.  This was confirmed with a laryngeal probe as well as use of mirror evaluated in the subglottic portion as well as the ventricle.  At this point, the scope was desuspended and the microscope was removed.  The scope was withdrawn through the vallecular region.  Inspection of the vallecula revealed a fullness on the right side with a papillomatous type growth that appeared very friable.  Biopsies were obtained with straight-biting cup forceps.  Once hemostasis was achieved, the scope was advanced into the piriform sinuses.  Again in the right piriform sinus, there was noted to be studding along the right lateral wall of the piriform sinus.  Again, biopsies were performed and once hemostasis was achieved, the scope was further withdrawn down the lateral pharyngeal wall.  There were no mucosal abnormalities identified within the oropharynx.  The scope was then completely removed and a bimanual examination was performed.  No neck masses were identified.  At this point, the procedure was complete.  The mouth guard was removed and the patient was returned to Anesthesia for awakening and taken to the recovery room without incident.
